issues.item: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: The appraisal of feared uncontrollable rage is not well supported by the rest of the profile. There are no corresponding trigger, threat, memory, or strategy items suggesting anger-driven reactivity, aggression risk, or conflict; the other appraisals instead center on shame and hopelessness after rape. This makes the rage item clinically discordant within the selected five components.

issues.item: Constant Socialising: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts
issues.explanation: The strategy of constant socialising is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile in this rape-related presentation. The selected triggers are solitary/sensory reminders (silence, outdoor smells, anniversary), and the appraisals are shame, suicidality, and feared rage. Constantly surrounding oneself with people does not connect clearly to these reminders and is somewhat at odds with body shame after rape, making it the least coherent avoidance/coping item here.

vignette:
Aminata was 74, an African woman who had spent most of her life working the land, and when she first came for help she spoke in the calm, spare way of someone used to carrying hardship without complaint. The assault had happened years earlier, while she was alone outdoors on the edge of the fields after dusk, the day's work nearly done and the air heavy with the smell of soil and plants. She had been raped in that setting, with the darkness closing in around her and the ordinary sounds of the day gone quiet. What stayed with her most was not only the violence itself but the particular stillness around it, the sudden sense that nothing and no one was coming. Since then, certain things had become unbearable in a way she struggled to explain to others. The smell of earth after rain, the familiar outdoor scent that once belonged to her work, could catch her off guard and bring the scene back so sharply that she would pause in the middle of a task, momentarily unable to stay present. Sudden or complete silence had the same effect; if the yard or house went quiet unexpectedly, she would stiffen and listen, as though her body were trying to decide whether something terrible was about to happen again. The anniversary of the assault was especially difficult. Each year as that date approached, she became more tense and withdrawn, already dreading a time she marked even when she tried not to.

In the months and years that followed, Aminata began organizing her life around what she could endure. She avoided being in circumstances that reminded her of the event, especially being in the dark, and after sunset she increasingly stayed close to lighted rooms or simply remained inside rather than risk going out. She also avoided being touched by other people in almost any form. Family members and her partner had learned that she would pull back from a hand on her shoulder or recoil if someone tried to comfort her with an embrace. She did not describe this as anger toward them; rather, she seemed embarrassed by how automatic it was, as if her body had set a limit that she could not negotiate. Over time, these habits narrowed her world. In the agricultural work that had always structured her days, she kept to tasks she could do in open daylight and felt uneasy when the day stretched toward evening or when she had to pass through quieter stretches of the fields. Even in familiar surroundings, the smell of damp earth or a sudden hush in the yard could make her scan the space around her and hurry to finish what she was doing. At home, she tried to manage her distress by forcing herself to think only positive thoughts, telling herself that she must not dwell on what had happened. She could do this for short periods, but she described it as an effortful discipline rather than relief, a way of pushing one thought down so another could take its place.

What she said sat most heavily on her was the way the assault had changed how she felt about her own body and her own worth. She spoke with visible shame about feeling dirty or contaminated because of what happened, as though the violation had left something permanent on her. That sense of contamination made physical closeness especially hard, even with someone she trusted. At times she also said she was not sure her life was worth living anymore, a thought that came to her when the distress felt relentless and when she imagined that this altered version of herself was what remained for the rest of her life. She was not presenting with dramatic displays, but with a quiet exhaustion and a guardedness that had become familiar to those around her. Her partner had noticed how often she turned down touches and how much her world had shrunk around daylight routines and avoidance of the dark, and the cumulative effect had been strain in a relationship that mattered to her.

By the time she sought help, the approaching anniversary was again near, and she found herself bracing against the familiar return of the worst days. The smell of soil in the fields and the hush that could fall over a room were still enough to jolt her into the memory she had spent years trying to push away. She came because she was tired of living as if every touch might threaten her, and because the thought that her life might no longer be worth living frightened her even more than the memory itself. What she hoped for, even if cautiously, was some way to feel clean again, to stand in her work without constantly bracing for what her senses might bring back, and to remain close to the person she loved without feeling forced to flinch away.
